title: Lab operations: a cheap cloud account and a safe state store
summary: Two operations stories: an off-site watchdog on a Free-plan AWS account without a surprise bill, and making the store that holds my Terraform state safe to rotate and rebuild.

stat.label: a month for the off-site watchdog: one function, one table and one schedule rule

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My lab runs on hardware in my home, so a power or internet outage silences the monitoring that would report it. I wanted a watcher outside the house, and a home for this site, on an AWS account with credit that expires in spring 2027.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: The watchdog is one Lambda function. The lab sends it a heartbeat every two minutes. A scheduled run of the same function posts a message to my Discord when the heartbeat stops, and probes the lab's public endpoints. It uses one on-demand table, one schedule rule and three parameters, and I wrote it in Terraform like the rest of the lab.

The site is a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront with origin access control and a certificate. A custom response-headers policy sets a content security policy and HSTS. DNS stays at Cloudflare, so the account uses no Route 53. The module is written so it stays inside the always-free allowance.

I wrote the account rules down before the first resource existed. I did not join an AWS Organization, and I use no Control Tower and no advanced features, because any of them ends credit earning. Free-plan-eligible services only, at the smallest sizes. A permissions boundary on the Terraform user stops it from creating a role more powerful than itself. A small monthly budget watches real money, a second budget counts credit burn, and anomaly detection emails me.

sections.heading: Trade-off
paragraphs: The deploy pipeline was designed around GitHub's OIDC login, so no long-lived key would exist. The account's organization has a service control policy that denies creating an OIDC provider, and a Free-plan account cannot lift it. I changed the design instead of working around the policy. The deploy identity is now a deploy-only IAM user with the same narrow policy. Terraform never creates its access key, so no secret reaches state. A script I run by hand creates the key and stores it as secrets on a protected environment that only the main branch may deploy to.
That is a weaker design than OIDC, and I chose it knowingly. The key can be rotated with one command, and the module switches back to OIDC with one variable on any account that allows it.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The watchdog is deployed. The lab's heartbeat reaches it, and its daily "alive" message arrived in my Discord on 3 November.

The site deploys from a merge to the main branch. The first deploy ran on 3 November: it type-checked, tested and built the site, confirmed which identity it ran as, synced the built files to S3 and invalidated the CloudFront cache. I then read the site back through CloudFront's own address: the home page and the case-study pages return 200 with the HSTS header, and a missing page returns the 404 page. The read-back also found that extensionless URLs such as /work returned 404, because the build writes work.html. A small CloudFront function now maps /work to /work.html.
The site now serves from the AWS copy at pdlab.dev. One part is still open: replacing the deploy user's long-lived key with a short-lived credential. I treat the key as a stopgap, not the design.

sections.heading: The state store
paragraphs: The same discipline applied at home. The object store that holds every Terraform state had an exposed credential and an Ansible role that no longer matched the running host, so running the role would have repointed the backend.

sections.heading: State store: what I did
paragraphs: First, a script rotates the exposed root credential and records the new one in the secrets store. Its first version rolled back every time, because its health check called a tool that the host does not have. A pull request switched the check to a language the host does have, and the rotation now holds.
Second, I found the vendor download site returns Gone for the pinned binary, so rebuilding the host from scratch would have failed. The role now fetches its binaries from a release in my own mirror.

Third, I made the role describe the running host exactly: its service account, environment file, service unit layout and firewall setting. A dry run with diffs is how I found each mismatch, and I fixed them one pull request at a time until the diff was clean. Other hosts keep the role's normal defaults.

sections.heading: State store: lesson
paragraphs: A configuration role that has drifted from reality is worse than none, because it looks like documentation and acts like a command. Make it match what is running, prove it with a dry run, and then it becomes a safe path to a rebuild.

sections.heading: What I would do differently
paragraphs: Check the account's policy limits before designing the auth. A short test that tries to create the OIDC provider would have found the block on the first day.

The exit plan is dated. The Free plan ends in April 2027, and a reminder fires two weeks before. By then I either upgrade with a budget alert in place, which should cost cents a month for a static site, or move the site to free static hosting and delete the bucket and distribution so nothing bills.
